mekki-muskil:107-107.t:
His saying {مَا دَامَت السَّمَاوَات وَالْأَرْض}: مَا is an adverb (ẓarf) in the position of accusative; its implied form is "the time of the lasting of the heavens and the earth".
His saying {إِلَّا مَا شَاءَ رَبك}: مَا is in the position of accusative as an exception (istithnāʾ) that is not from [the genus of] the first.

mekki-muskil:108-108.t: His saying {وَأما الَّذين سعدوا}: the reading of Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza is with ḍamma on the sīn (سُعِدوا), on the analogy of their saying مَسْعُود, and it is a rare, anomalous (shādhdh) usage. Their saying مَسْعُود came only by dropping the augment, as though from أسعده الله, while one does not say سعده الله; so it is like their saying أجنه الله فَهُوَ مَجْنُون: مجنون came on the pattern of جنه الله even though that is not said; likewise مَسْعُود came on the pattern of سعده الله even though that is not said. The ḍamma on the sīn in سعدوا is far-fetched according to most grammarians, except on the assumption of dropping the augment, as though He said وَأما الَّذين أسعدوا.

mekki-muskil:111-111.t:
His saying {وَإِن كلا لما ليوفينهم}: whoever reads إن with shadda brings it in its original form and makes it govern كل; the lām in لما is a lām of emphasis entering on مَا, which is the khabar (predicate) of إن, and ليوفينهم is the answer to the oath. Its implied form is: "and indeed all are a creation — or are human beings — whom He will surely pay in full (وَإِن كلا لخلق أَو لبشر ليوفينهم)". It is not good for مَا to be redundant (zāʾida), for then the lām would be entering on ليوفينهم, and its entering on the lām of the oath is not permissible. It has been said that مَا is redundant, but entered to separate between the two lāms that receive the oath, both of which are with fatḥa, so they were separated by مَا.
As for whoever lightens إن, he lightened it out of finding the doubling heavy, and made it govern كل just as it governs when doubled, and the lām in لما remains as it is.
As for the doubling of لمّا in the reading of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir, its origin is لمن مَا; then the nūn was assimilated into the mīm, so three mīms came together in pronunciation, and the mīm with kasra was dropped. Its implied form is: "and indeed all are of those whom He created; your Lord will surely pay them in full (وان كلا لمن خلق ليوفينهم رَبك)". It has also been said that the implied form is لمَن مَا, with fatḥa on the mīm of من, so that مَا is redundant, and one of the mīms is dropped because of the repetition of the mīm in pronunciation, as we have mentioned; so the implied form is "for a creation whom He will surely pay in full (لخلق ليوفينهم)".
It has been said that لمّا in this place is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of لمّ ("to gather"), but it was treated in continuous speech as it is treated in pausal form; this is far-fetched, because treating something in continuous speech as it is treated in pause is permissible only in poetry. It has been related that al-Kisāʾī said: "I do not know the rationale for the doubling in لمّا." Al-Zuhrī read لمًّا, doubled and with nunation, as the maṣdar of لمّ.
If you made إن, in the state of lightening, mean مَا (negation), you would put كل in the nominative, and the doubling in لمّا would carry the meaning of إِلَّا ("except"), as He said إِن كل نفس لما عَلَيْهَا, meaning "there is no soul but that over it…", according to the reading of whoever doubles لمّا. In the codex (ḥarf) of Ubayy: وَإِن كل إِلَّا ليوفينهم, with إن meaning مَا. Al-Aʿmash read وَإِن كل لما ليوفينهم, making إن mean مَا and لمّا mean إِلَّا, with كل in the nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject) in all of that and ليوفينهم as the khabar. It has also been said that مَا is redundant in the reading of whoever lightens [لما], and ليوفينهم is the khabar.

mekki-muskil:116-116.t:
His saying {إِلَّا قَلِيلا مِمَّن أنجينا مِنْهُم}: accusative as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). Al-Farrāʾ permitted the nominative in it as a badal (substitute) from أولو; in his view it is like His saying إِلَّا قوم يُونُس: it is a disconnected exception, and in his view the nominative is permissible in it as a substitute, as [the poet] said:
... وبدلة لَيْسَ بهَا أنيس ... إِلَّا اليعافير والا العيس ...
(And many a land with no companion in it, except young gazelles and white camels.)
He put اليعافير in the nominative as a substitute from أنيس, whereas its due is the accusative, because it is a disconnected exception from the sentence.

mekki-muskil:87-87.t: His saying {أَو أَن نَفْعل فِي أَمْوَالنَا مَا نشَاء}: whoever reads it with the nūn in both [verbs] conjoins it to the object of نَتْرُك, which is مَا; it is not permissible to conjoin it to the object of تأمرك, which is أَن, because the meaning would change. Whoever reads مَا تشَاء with the tāʾ, then أَو أَن نَفْعل is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to the object of تأمرك, which is أَن, unlike the first view. Whoever reads تفعل and تشاء with the tāʾ in both, it is permissible to conjoin أَو أَن تفعل to the object of نَتْرُك, which is مَا, and to the object of تأمرك, which is أَن. We have explained this verse on its own in another book.

mekki-muskil:89-89.t: His saying {شقاقي}: its meaning is "my opposition (مشاقي)", and it is in the position of nominative (marfūʿ) as the agent of يجرمنكم.

mekki-muskil:91-91.t: His saying {ضَعِيفا}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the kāf in نرَاك, because it is from seeing with the eye.

mekki-muskil:93-93.t: His saying {من يَأْتِيهِ}: من is in the position of accusative (manṣūb) by تعلمون. In meaning it is like وَالله يعلم الْمُفْسد من المصلح, i.e. He knows these two kinds; likewise the meaning in the verse is: you will come to know these two kinds. Al-Farrāʾ permitted من to be interrogative, in which case it is in the position of nominative. The fact that the second من is a relative noun indicates that the first is also a relative noun and not an interrogative.

mekki-muskil:1-1.t: If you make هود a name for the sūra and say هذه هود ("this is Hūd"), it is a diptote according to Sībawayh and al-Khalīl, like a woman whom you named Zayd or ʿAmr. ʿĪsā [ibn ʿUmar] allowed it to be fully declined because of its lightness, just as هند, the name of a woman, is declined. If you assume the omission of a muḍāf (first term of a genitive construct) with هود, you decline it, meaning "this is the sūra of Hūd".

mekki-muskil:11-11.t: His saying {إِلَّا الَّذين صَبَرُوا}: الذين is in the position of the accusative as a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil). Al-Farrāʾ said: it is excepted from الإنسان, because that has the meaning of "people". Al-Akhfash said: it is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ).

mekki-muskil:16-16.t: His saying {وباطل مَا كَانُوا يعْملُونَ}: باطل is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject) and what follows it is its khabar (predicate). In the ḥarf (reading) of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd it is وباطلاً in the accusative: they made ما redundant (zāʾida) and made باطلا accusative by يعملون, like قليلا ما تذكرون and قليلا ما تؤمنون.

mekki-muskil:17-17.t:
His saying {ويتلوه شَاهد}: the hāʾ in يتلوه is for the Qurʾān; on this view the hāʾ in منه is for Allah, exalted be His mention, and the witness is the Gospel, i.e. the Gospel from Allah follows the Qurʾān in being placed before it; so the hāʾ in قبله is also for the Gospel. It has been said that the hāʾ in يتلوه is for Muhammad, Allah bless him; then the witness is his tongue, and the hāʾ in منه is also for Muhammad, Allah bless him — and it has been said: for the Qurʾān — and likewise the hāʾ in قبله is for Muhammad, Allah bless him. It has been said that the witness is Gabriel, upon him be peace; on this view the hāʾ in منه is for Allah the Exalted, and in من قبله it is also for Gabriel. It has been said that the witness is the inimitability of the Qurʾān; on this view the hāʾ in منه is for Allah the Exalted, the hāʾ in قبله is for the Qurʾān, and the hāʾ in يؤمنون به is for the Qurʾān — and it has been said: for Muhammad, upon him be peace.
His saying {إِمَامًا وَرَحْمَة}: accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from كتاب موسى.

mekki-muskil:20-20.t: His saying {مَا كَانُوا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ السّمع}: ما is an adverb (ẓarf) in the position of the accusative; its meaning is "as long as", for ever. It has been said that ما is in the position of the accusative by omission of the preposition, i.e. "for what they used to…" (بما كانوا), just as one says جزيته ما فعل and بما فعل ("I repaid him [for] what he did"). It has been said that ما is negating, and the meaning is "they could not hear because of what had preceded for them [in decree]". And it has been said that the meaning is: they could not bear to hear from the Prophet, Allah bless him, because of their hatred of him, nor understand an argument — as you say "so-and-so cannot bear to look at so-and-so" when that is burdensome to him.

mekki-muskil:22-22.t:
His saying {لَا جرم أَنهم}: لا جرم according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh has the meaning of "truly" (حقا), in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject); لا and جرم are a single word, made indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and the khabar (predicate) is أنهم; so أنّ is in the position of the nominative according to both of them. It is also reported of al-Khalīl that he said: أنّ is in the position of the nominative by جرم, and جرم has the meaning of بُدّ, so its meaning is "no escape" and "inevitably". Al-Khalīl said: لا was brought so that it be known that the addressee did not begin his speech, but was only answering one who had addressed him. Al-Zajjāj said: لا is a negation of what they thought would benefit them. The original meaning of جرم is "earned", from their saying فلان جارم أهله, i.e. their earner; from it a sin is called جرم, because it is earned. So the meaning according to him is: "that does not benefit them"; then He began and said جرم أنهم في الآخرة هم الأخسرون, i.e. that deed earned them loss in the Hereafter; so on this view أنّ of أنهم is in the position of the accusative by جرم. Al-Kisāʾī said: its meaning is "there is no turning away and no preventing from their being in the Hereafter…", so أنّ on his view too is in the position of the accusative, by omission of the preposition.
«[Translator's note: the text reads «لاصد», evidently for «لا صدّ».]»

mekki-muskil:27-27.t:
His saying {بَادِي الرَّأْي}: بادي is accusative as an adverb (ẓarf), i.e. "in the first appearance of opinion"; this is on the reading of whoever does not pronounce it with hamza. It is also permissible for it to be a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) with which a preposition has been omitted, like واختار موسى قومه. فاعل was permitted to be an adverb only as that is permitted for فعيل, such as قريب and مليء; فاعل and فعيل alternate, such as راحم and رحيم, عالم and عليم. That is good in فاعل because it is annexed to الرأي, and الرأي is something to which a maṣdar (verbal noun) is annexed, with the maṣdar becoming accusative with it as an adverb, as in your saying أما جهدَ رأيي فإنك منطلق ("as for my best opinion, you are leaving"). What governs the adverb is اتبعك. It is from بدا يبدو when something appears. In the reading of whoever does not use hamza it is also permissible for it to be from beginning (الابتداء), but he lightened the hamza. Whoever reads it with hamza, or assumes that the alif is a substitute for a hamza, also has it accusative as an adverb, and what governs it is again اتبعك.
So the implied form according to the one who takes it from بدا يبدو is: "No one has followed you, O Noah, except the lowest, as far as appears to us of opinion", as though they decided against him at the first that appeared to them of their opinion and did not follow it up with consideration; they only said what appeared to them without certainty. The implied form according to the one who takes it from beginning, and so uses hamza, is: "No one has followed you, O Noah, except the lowest at the start of the matter", i.e. "we do not see that, at the start of the matter, anyone followed you except the lowest".
The adverb was permitted to come late, after إلا and what follows it of the agent and its complement, because with adverbs a latitude is allowed that is not allowed with objects. If you said in ordinary speech ما أعطيت أحدا إلا زيدا درهما ("I gave no one except Zayd a dirham"), placing two nouns as objects after إلا, it would not be permissible, because the verb does not reach two nouns by means of إلا; it reaches only one noun, like the other particles. Do you not see that if you said مررت بزيد عمرو, making the verb reach both by one particle, it would not be permissible? Likewise if you said استوى الماء والخشبة الحائط, making two nouns accusative by one wāw, it would not be permissible — unless in all of that you bring the conjunctive wāw, and then it is permissible, and the verb reaches both by two particles. As for their saying ما ضرب القوم إلا بعضهم بعضا ("the people did not strike, except some of them [struck] others"), it was permitted only because بعضهم is a badal (substitute) from القوم, so the verb did not reach, after إلا, more than one noun.
«[Translator's note: the sentence «فالتقدير عنه قد جعله من بدأ يبدو» is as printed; «عنه» is evidently for «عند من». It is translated accordingly.]»

mekki-muskil:28-28.t:
His saying {فعميت عَلَيْكُم}: whoever among the readers reads it without doubling takes it in the sense of "you were blind to the reports that came to you", which are the mercy, so you did not believe in them; the reports themselves were not blind to them — had they been blind, they would have had an excuse in that; it is only they who were blind to them. So it is an inversion (maqlūb), like their saying أدخلت القلنسوة في رأسي ("I put the cap into my head") and أدخلت القبر زيدا ("I put the grave into Zayd"); you said all of this according to the outward wording, because the meaning is not obscure. Similar to it is the saying of the Exalted فلا تحسبن الله مخلف وعده رسله. It has been said that the meaning of فعميت, for the one who reads it without doubling, is "it was hidden"; on this view it is not inverted, and the reports that came from Allah — their understanding was hidden from them because of their little concern for them and their frequent turning away from them.
As for its meaning in the reading of Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, who read it with doubling and ḍamma as a passive (فعُمِّيت), there is no inversion in it; rather, Allah made it blind to them because of the wretchedness He intended for them — He does what He wills, glory be to Him. This goes back to the first reading, because they were not blind to it until Allah made it blind to them. Ubayy read — and it is the reading of al-Aʿmash — فعمّاها عليكم, i.e. "Allah made it blind to you"; this is evidence for whoever reads with ḍamma and doubling.
نوح, the name of the Prophet, upon him be peace, is fully declined because it is foreign and light. It has been said that it is Arabic, from ناح ينوح ("to lament"); some of the exegetes said: he was named Noah only because of his much lamenting over himself.

mekki-muskil:31-31.t: His saying {تزدري أعينكُم}: the original of تزدري is تزتري; the dāl is a substitute for a tāʾ, because the dāl is a voiced letter, so it was paired with the zāy, since that is also voiced, whereas the tāʾ is voiceless and so differs from the zāy; the substitution was good because the two points of articulation are close. The implied form is تزدريهم أعينكم ("your eyes look down on them"); then the pronoun was omitted because of the length of the noun.

mekki-muskil:36-36.t: His saying {إِلَّا من قد آمن}: من is in the position of the nominative by يؤمن.

mekki-muskil:40-40.t: His saying {وَمن آمن}: من is in the position of the accusative by conjunction with اثنين or with أهلك. And من in His saying إلا من سبق is in the position of the accusative as excepted from الأهل.

mekki-muskil:41-41.t:
His saying {بِسم الله مجْراهَا وَمرْسَاهَا}: مجراها is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), مرساها is conjoined to it, and the khabar (predicate) is بسم الله; the implied form is "in the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring". It is permissible for both to be nominative by the prepositional phrase (ẓarf), because it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to what precedes it, namely اركبوا. It is also permissible for مجراها to be in the position of the accusative as an adverb (ẓarf), on the assumption of the omission of an adverb annexed to مجراها, in the manner of your saying آتيك مقدم الحاج ("I will come to you at the arrival of the pilgrims"), i.e. at the time of the arrival of the pilgrims; then the implied form is "in the name of Allah at the time of its sailing and its anchoring". It has been said that its implied form in the accusative is "in the name of Allah at the place of its sailing", and then the muḍāf was omitted. In the exegesis there is what indicates its accusative as an adverb: al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: at the time of its sailing he would say "In the name of Allah", and it would sail; and at the time of its anchoring "In the name of Allah", and it would anchor.
The bāʾ in بسم الله is attached to اركبوا. What governs مجراها, when it is an adverb, is the sense of the prepositional phrase in بسم الله; اركبوا does not govern it, because He did not mean "embark in it at the time of sailing and anchoring"; the meaning is only "say the name of Allah at the time of sailing and anchoring", and the implied form is "embark now, seeking blessing in the name of Allah at the time of sailing and anchoring".
If you make مجراها nominative as a mubtadaʾ with what precedes it as its khabar, the clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in فيها, because in the clause there is a referent (ʿāʾid) referring back to the hāʾ in فيها, namely the hāʾ in مجراها, since both are for the ship; and what governs the clause that is a ḥāl is the verbal sense contained in فيها. It is not good for this clause to be in the position of a ḥāl from the implied pronoun in اركبوا, because there is no referent in the clause referring back to the pronoun in اركبوا: the pronoun in بسم الله, if you make it the khabar of مجراها, refers only back to the mubtadaʾ, which is مجراها; and if you make مجراها nominative by the prepositional phrase, there is no pronoun in it; and the hāʾ in مجراها refers only back to the hāʾ in فيها.
If you make مجراها accusative as an adverb, بسم الله governs it, and the clause is in the position of a ḥāl from the implied pronoun in اركبوا, on the assumption of your saying خرج بثيابه ("he went out in his clothes") and ركب بسلاحه ("he rode with his weapons"); and from it is His saying وقد دخلوا بالكفر وهم قد خرجوا به: your sayings بثيابه, بسلاحه, بالكفر and به are all in the position of a ḥāl. So likewise بسم الله مجراها is in the position of a ḥāl from the implied pronoun in اركبوا when you make مجراها accusative as an adverb; its implied form is "embark in it, seeking blessing in the name of Allah at the time of sailing and anchoring". Then in بسم الله there is a pronoun referring back to the implied pronoun in اركبوا, which is the pronoun of those commanded, so the ḥāl from them is sound because of the pronoun that refers back to them. On this assumption it is not good for the clause to be in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun, which is the hāʾ in فيها, because there is no referent referring back to the owner of the ḥāl; and the pronoun in مجراها does not suffice, because it is not part of the ḥāl clause — it is only an idle (mulghā) adverb, and when it is idle the pronoun attached to it is not counted. مجراها would be part of the ḥāl clause only if you made it nominative as a mubtadaʾ. If you made the clause in the position of a ḥāl from the hāʾ in فيها while making مجراها accusative as an adverb, the implied form would become "embark in it [the ship] seeking blessing in the name of Allah at the time of sailing", and the meaning is not so: seeking blessing is not predicated of the ship; seeking blessing belongs only to those riding in it.
If you made مجراها and مرساها stand in the position of an active participle (ism fāʿil), it would be an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara), and that would be permissible, and you would make it in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the name of Allah the Exalted. It was an adverb in the preceding discussion only on the basis that مجراها is not made to stand in the position of an active participle; but if you make مجراها in the sense of جارية and مرساها in the sense of راسية, its being an anticipated ḥāl is good.
By this question one can come to understand everything like it in speech and in the Qurʾān — that is for whoever understands it as it should be understood and reflects on it as it should be reflected on; for it is among the choicest of difficult questions.
As for fatḥa and ḍamma on the mīm in مجراها: whoever reads with fatḥa takes the speech on جرت مجرى ("it sailed a sailing"), and whoever reads with ḍamma takes it on أجراها الله مجرى ("Allah made it sail a sailing"). ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read مجريها ومرسيها with yāʾ, making them both a naʿt (adjective) of Allah, exalted be His mention; it is also permissible for them to be in the position of the nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ, i.e. "He is its Sailer and its Anchorer".

mekki-muskil:42-42.t:
His saying {وَكَانَ فِي معزل}: whoever reads the zāy with kasra makes it a noun of place, and whoever reads it with fatḥa takes it as a maṣdar (verbal noun).
His saying {يَا بني اركب مَعنا}: the original of بني is with three yāʾs: the yāʾ of the diminutive; a yāʾ after it which is the third radical (lām al-fiʿl); and a yāʾ after the third radical which is the yāʾ of annexation (the first-person possessive). Therefore the third radical was given kasra, because the due of the yāʾ of annexation in the singular is that what precedes it always takes kasra. The yāʾ of the diminutive was assimilated into the third radical, because the due of the diminutive yāʾ is quiescence, and when two identical letters other than the letters of prolongation and softness come together and the first is quiescent, it must be assimilated into the second. The yāʾ of annexation was dropped because the kasra indicates it; dropping it in the vocative is most frequent in the speech of the Arabs, because it has taken the place of the nunation, and nunation in definite nouns does not remain in the vocative, so it became necessary to drop what is like the nunation and stands in its place, namely the yāʾ of annexation. Dropping it was strengthened in such a case by the meeting of burdensome identical letters together with the kasra, which is also heavy.
ʿĀṣim read it with fatḥa on the yāʾ. That is because he replaced the kasra of the third radical with a fatḥa, finding heavy the meeting of the yāʾs together with the kasra; so the yāʾ of annexation was changed into an alif, then the alif was dropped as the yāʾ is dropped, and the fatḥa remained as it was. Dropping the alif was strengthened because it is a compensation for what is dropped in the vocative, namely the yāʾ of annexation.
Ibn Kathīr read, in a place other than this, in Luqmān, with the yāʾ quiescent and lightened. That is because he dropped the yāʾ of annexation for the vocative, so a doubled yāʾ with kasra remained, and the kasra is like a yāʾ; this was found heavy, so he dropped the third radical, and the yāʾ of the diminutive remained quiescent.

mekki-muskil:43-43.t:
His saying {لَا عَاصِم الْيَوْم من أَمر الله}: what governs اليوم is من أمر الله, its implied form being "there is no protector from the command of Allah today". لا عاصم is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and من أمر الله is the khabar (predicate), with من attached (mutaʿalliq) to something omitted, its implied form being "there is no protector preventing from the command of Allah today". It is also permissible for من أمر الله to be an adjective of عاصم and to govern اليوم, with a khabar for عاصم implied. It is not permissible for من to be attached to عاصم, nor for اليوم to be made accusative by عاصم, because it would then be necessary to give عاصما nunation and not make it indeclinable on fatḥa, because whatever is attached to it and what it governs would become part of its completion, so it would become like your saying لا خيرا من زيد في الدار ("there is none better than Zayd in the house"). Its parallel is لا تثريب عليكم اليوم, which will come in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills.
His saying {إِلَّا من رحم}: من is in the position of the accusative as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), with عاصم in its proper sense; its implied form is "no one prevents [anyone] from the command of Allah, but whoever Allah has mercy on is protected". It has been said that من is in the position of the nominative as a badal (substitute) from the position of عاصم; that is on two assumptions. One of them is that عاصم is in its proper sense, so the implied form is "none protects today from the command of Allah except Allah" — and it has been said: "except the Merciful One", and the Merciful One is Allah, exalted be His mention. The second assumption is that عاصم has the meaning of معصوم ("protected"), so the implied form is "none is protected from the command of Allah today except the one shown mercy".

mekki-muskil:46-46.t:
His saying {إِنَّه عمل غير صَالح}: the hāʾ refers back to the request, i.e. "your asking Me to save a disbeliever is an unrighteous deed". It has been said that its meaning is "your asking about what you have no knowledge of is an unrighteous deed". On these two assumptions the wording is a saying of Allah to Noah, upon him be peace. It has been said that it is a saying of Noah, upon him be peace, to his son: that is, he said to him "Embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers; your being with the disbelievers is an unrighteous deed", so this is a saying of Noah to his son connected to what precedes it. It has been said that the hāʾ in إنه refers back to the son of Noah, and in the speech there is the omission of a muḍāf (first term of a genitive construct), its implied form being "your son is one of unrighteous deeds". As for the hāʾ in the reading of al-Kisāʾī, it refers back to the son without disagreement, because he read عمِلَ with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the lām, and غيرَ in the accusative.
«[Translator's note: the text reads «مصلا», evidently for «متصلا» ("connected").]»

mekki-muskil:50-50.t:
His saying {من إِلَه غَيره}: غير may be nominative as a naʿt (adjective) of, or a badal (substitute) from, the wording of إله [i.e. its position]; it has been read with both [the nominative and the genitive]. The accusative as an exception is also permissible.
«[Translator's note: the text says «من لفظ إله», though the nominative is on the position of إله, its wording being genitive; «وقد قرئ بهما» refers to the nominative and genitive readings.]»

mekki-muskil:52-52.t: His saying {مدرارا}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from السماء. Its origin is with the hāʾ [i.e. the feminine ending], but the Arabs drop the hāʾ from مفعال by way of relation (nasab).

mekki-muskil:64-64.t: His saying {لكم آيَة}: آية is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from الناقة.

mekki-muskil:66-66.t: His saying {وَمن خزي يَوْمئِذٍ}: whoever reads the mīm with fatḥa makes يوم indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, because of its annexation to an undeclinable word, namely إذ. Whoever reads the mīm with kasra declines it and puts it in the genitive, because الخزي is annexed to اليوم, and does not make it indeclinable.

mekki-muskil:67-67.t: His saying {وَأخذ الَّذين ظلمُوا الصَّيْحَة}: the tāʾ was dropped from أخذ only because the feminine noun, which is الصيحة, has been separated from its verb, which is أخذ, by His saying الذين ظلموا, which is the object of أخذ; so the separation stood in place of the feminine marker. At the end of the sūra, in the story of Shuʿayb, He said وأخذت, following the feminine according to the original and not counting the separation. It has been said that the tāʾ was dropped only because the femininity of الصيحة is not real, since it has no masculine from its own wording. And it has been said that the tāʾ was dropped only because it was taken according to the meaning of الصياح, since الصيحة and الصياح have the same meaning. Likewise is the reason in everything that resembles it.

mekki-muskil:69-69.t:
His saying {قَالُوا سَلاما}: سلاما is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun). It has been said that it is made accusative by قالوا, as you say قلت خيرا ("I said good"), because their speech is not quoted; السلام is only the meaning of what they said, so the verb "say" was made to govern it — just as you say قلت حقا ("I said: true") to someone you heard saying "There is no god but Allah": you did not mention what he said, you only brought a word that confirms his saying, so you made "say" govern it. Likewise سلام in the verse is only the meaning of what they said; it is not their very wording to be quoted. Had it been nominative, it would be quoted and would be their very words. So the accusative, always, in this and the like with the verb "say", is only the meaning of what they said, not their very words; and the nominative is on the basis that it is their very words, quoted from them.
His saying {قَالَ سَلام}: nominative as quotation of their speech; it is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), or a mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "he said: it is peace", or "my affair is peace", or "upon you be peace". Making both accusative is permissible according to what has preceded, and making both nominative is permissible by quotation and implying.
His saying {فَمَا لبث أَن جَاءَ}: أن is in the position of the accusative on the assumption of the omission of the preposition, its implied form being "he did not delay in coming" (عن أن جاء). Al-Farrāʾ allowed it to be in the position of the nominative by لبث; its implied form according to him is "his coming did not delay", i.e. his coming with a calf was not slow. So on the first view لبث contains the pronoun of Abraham, and on the second view there is no pronoun in it. It has been said that ما has the meaning of الذي, and in the speech there is the omission of a muḍāf (first term of a genitive construct), its implied form being "and what Abraham tarried was the measure of his coming with a calf" — he wanted to show the extent of his delay; so لبث contains the agent pronoun, which is also Abraham.

mekki-muskil:71-71.t:
His saying {وَمن وَرَاء إِسْحَاق يَعْقُوب}: whoever reads يعقوب in the nominative makes it a mubtadaʾ (subject) with what precedes it as its khabar (predicate), and the clause is in the position of the accusative as an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara) from the implied accusative pronoun in بشرناها; then يعقوب is included in the good tidings. It is permissible to make يعقوب nominative by implying a verb, its implied form being "and after Isaac comes into being (يحدث) Jacob"; then يعقوب is not included in the good tidings.
Whoever reads يعقوب in the accusative makes it in the position of the genitive, by conjunction with إسحاق, but it is a diptote because of definiteness and foreignness; this is the view of al-Kisāʾī. It is weak according to Sībawayh and al-Akhfash unless the preposition is repeated, because you have separated the preposition [i.e. what stands for it] from its genitive noun by the prepositional phrase, and the due of the genitive noun is to be adjacent to the preposition, and the wāw has stood in place of the preposition. Do you not see that if you said مررت بزيد وفي الدار عمرو it would be ugly, and the right expression is مررت بزيد وعمرو في الدار, and بشرناها بإسحاق ويعقوب من ورائه? It has been said that يعقوب is accusative, construed on the position of بإسحاق; this too is far-fetched, because of the separation between the conjunction and the conjoined word by His saying ومن وراء إسحاق, as was the case with the genitive. On these two views يعقوب is included in the good tidings. It has been said that it is accusative by an implied verb indicated by the speech, its implied form being "and after Isaac We granted him Jacob"; then it is not included in the good tidings.
«[Translator's note: the text reads «ويحث», evidently for «ويحدث», and is translated accordingly.]»

mekki-muskil:72-72.t: His saying {وَهَذَا بعلي شَيخا}: شيخ is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the one pointed to, and what governs the ḥāl is the pointing and the alerting [contained in the demonstrative]. This pointing is permissible only when the addressee knows the owner of the ḥāl, so that the benefit of the statement lies in the ḥāl. If he does not know the owner of the ḥāl, the benefit of the statement lies only in knowing the owner of the ḥāl, and a ḥāl may not occur for him, because the meaning would become that he is so-and-so in one state and not in another. If you said هذا زيد قائما ("this is Zayd, standing") to someone who does not know Zayd, it would not be permissible, because you would be telling him that the one pointed to is Zayd in the state of his standing, so that if he ceased standing he would not be Zayd. When the addressee knows Zayd himself, you have informed him only of the occurrence of the ḥāl from him; and when he does not know him himself, you have informed him only of who he is, so no ḥāl occurs from him, for the reason we mentioned. The nominative in شيخ is permissible in five ways, which we have left unmentioned because they are well known.

mekki-muskil:74-74.t: His saying {وجاءته الْبُشْرَى يجادلنا}: the view of al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī is that يجادلنا stands in the place of جادلنا, because the apodosis (jawāb) of لمّا must be a past verb, so the imperfect was put in its place — just as the due of the apodosis of a condition is to be imperfect, yet the past is put in its place. It has been said that the meaning is "he set about disputing with Us", so it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from Abraham, upon him be peace.

mekki-muskil:78-78.t:
His saying {هن أطهر لكم}: a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate); nothing else is permissible according to the Basrans. It is related that ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read أطهرَ in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), making هن a separating pronoun (fāṣila); that is far-fetched and weak.
His saying {ضَيْفِي}: its origin is a maṣdar (verbal noun); therefore it is not put in the dual or the plural.

mekki-muskil:81-81.t:
His saying {إِلَّا امْرَأَتك}: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read it in the nominative, as a badal (substitute) from أحد. Abū ʿUbayd rejected the nominative as a badal and said: on this basis يلتفت would have to be nominative, making لا a negation; for if you substitute the woman for أحد and put يلتفت in the jussive as a prohibition, the meaning becomes that the woman was permitted to turn round, and that is not permissible; according to him the badal is not sound except with يلتفت in the nominative, and no one read it so. Al-Mubarrad said: the justification of this reading is that what is meant by the prohibition is the addressee, while its wording is directed to someone else — as you say to your servant لا يخرج فلان ("let so-and-so not go out"): the wording of the prohibition is for so-and-so, but its meaning is for the addressee, so its meaning is "do not let him go out". Likewise the meaning of the prohibition is only for Lot, i.e. "do not let them turn round, except your wife". Likewise your saying لا يقم أحد إلا زيد means "forbid them from standing, except Zayd".
As for the accusative in امرأتك, it is as an exception, because it is a prohibition and not a negation. It is also permissible for it to be excepted from His saying فأسر بأهلك — "except your wife"; on this view only the accusative is permissible for the woman, if you make her excepted from الأهل. The exception after the prohibition is good only because it is a complete statement, just as your saying جاءني القوم ("the people came to me") is a complete statement; then you say إلا زيد ("except Zayd"), making an exception and using the accusative.
«[Translator's note: the text writes «إلا زيد» without the accusative ending, though it speaks of the accusative.]»
